title: Structure-First Interpretability: Anchoring Sparse Autoencoders to the Daopology Knowledge Base
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become the dominant tool for decomposing large language model (LLM) activations into interpretable features. Yet the field faces a fundamental crisis: there is no ground truth for what concepts a model actually uses, and a growing body of evidence shows that SAE-learned dictionaries point in substantially wrong directions, that SAE explanations suffer from descriptive collision at scale, and that SAE features fail to improve downstream tasks beyond simple baselines. This paper argues that the root cause is the absence of an external semantic reference frame—SAEs operate without an anchor. We propose a methodology that anchors SAE research to Daopology, an axiomatic system that provides 79 minimal expressive parameters for structuring knowledge across seven categories: 9 primitives, 6 Heng families, 6 Jiao families, 8 Cha families, 7 Que families, 10 Suan families, and 21 He families. We further introduce GlyphCode, a universal symbolic encoding system that renders structural entities as compositional symbol trees, and the GlyphCode Reasoner, a neuro-symbolic inference engine that operates on these trees. The proposed “structure-first” paradigm reverses the current practice: instead of asking “what does this SAE feature mean?”, we ask “which Daopology structure does this SAE feature align with?” We outline four concrete interventions—structural initialization, structural regularization, causal verification via stability criteria, and cross-model alignment via kernel isomorphism—and provide a set of falsifiable predictions. The paper positions itself as a methodology contribution, arguing that the path forward for mechanistic interpretability lies not in scaling SAEs further, but in providing them with the semantic scaffolding they currently lack.

title: Cryptography-Driven-Deterministic-Logical-Timeline-Dual-Timestamp
abstract: An AI behavior auditing system based on a deterministic logical timeline binds cryptographic states to logical moments, making every AI decision traceable, independently verifiable, and infinitely replayable. When this system is applied to scenarios involving external large-model API calls, three engineering problems arise: an API call spans multiple logical ticks while the behavior record binds only the request moment; a single mode of logical counter advancement cannot accommodate intermittent calls and continuous monitoring; and concurrent recording across multiple physical media lacks architectural guidance. This paper proposes a request-receipt dual-timestamp binding mechanism, three trigger modes (periodic, event, and hybrid), and a multi-physical-time-axis concurrent recording architecture. It provides complete data structures, algorithm flows, auditing methods, and experimental data, as prior art for free use by the industry. This paper also explicitly delineates the security boundaries and trust assumptions of each mechanism, and provides engineering implementation schemes for authentication tag construction, clock trust models, and cross-axis causality proofs.

title: Hypergraph-Augmented Reconstruction and Adaptive Metric Aggregation Network for Few-Shot Fine-Grained Image Classification
abstract: Few-shot fine-grained image classification aims to recognize unseen fine-grained categories from very few labeled examples. The task is difficult because visually similar classes may differ only in subtle details, while images from the same class can vary considerably. Useful evidence is therefore often localized. Reconstruction-based metric methods reduce local misalignment by reconstructing query features from class-wise support features, but a small support set may still provide an incomplete reconstruction basis. In addition, spatial reconstruction errors are usually combined with fixed or nearly uniform weights, and intermediate features receive no direct reconstruction-oriented supervision. We develop HARA, a Hypergraph-Augmented Reconstruction and Adaptive Metric Aggregation Network, to address these limitations. HARA forms learnable soft hyperedges over local support features and uses the resulting aggregated features to enrich the class-wise reconstruction basis. It then combines class-conditional reconstruction with query self-reconstruction to obtain position-wise joint errors, which are aggregated using query-dependent weights. A training-only auxiliary branch applies reconstruction-based supervision to intermediate backbone features. For 5-way evaluation, HARA obtains 84.09%/93.48% on CUB-200-2011, 76.91%/88.69% on Stanford Dogs and 88.53%/95.87% on Stanford Cars under the 1-shot/5-shot settings, respectively. Ablation and diagnostic analyses further characterize the contributions and behavior of the proposed framework. Overall, HARA provides an effective extension to reconstruction-based few-shot fine-grained classification.

title: On the Theoretical Limits of Learning Unconstrained Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) accelerate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations by learning the energies and forces that govern atomic motion. Recent work has shown that relaxing physical inductive biases can improve computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, raising the question of whether energy-and-force matching alone is sufficient to ensure accurate sampling. We show that, for unconstrained hypothesis classes, the relationship between prediction error and sampling accuracy is exponentially ill-conditioned in dimension. In particular, prediction errors that decay exponentially with dimension can coexist with nearly maximal total variation distance between the learned and target distributions. We identify two failure mechanisms. The first is kinetic trapping, where relaxation to an accurate learned equilibrium requires exponentially long times, even when simulations are initialized from training configurations at which energies and forces are matched exactly. The second is equilibrium mismatch, where the learned stationary distribution itself remains far from the target. Under explicit assumptions, we show that equilibrium mismatch can persist even in local, symmetry-preserving models, where small per-atom errors coexist with a distributional discrepancy that approaches its maximum as system size increases. Finally, we establish global energy-control conditions that guarantee equilibrium accuracy and identify additional conditions required for rapid relaxation.

title: Dissecting the Carbon-SLO Tension in Geo-Distributed LLM Serving
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) inference is driving a growing share of datacenter carbon emissions. Although carbon-aware scheduling can reduce these emissions in geo-distributed datacenters by exploiting the spatiotemporal variations in grid carbon intensity, the latency-sensitive nature of LLM serving constrains this design space. While prior studies investigate the carbon savings achievable through spatial scheduling, they oversimplify the dynamics of modern inference engines, such as queueing and continuous batching, which strongly shape inference latency. We address this issue by designing and evaluating a latency-centric, geo-distributed inference simulator, calibrated with hardware-grounded latency and power measurements, that reproduces these dynamics and enables the study of carbon savings under strict service-level objectives (SLOs). We then formulate a series of SLO- and carbon-aware schedulers of increasing sophistication, from per-request heuristics to batch-level optimization: (i) a greedy heuristic, (ii) an integer linear programming (ILP)-based scheduler jointly assigning batches of requests, (iii) an iterative ILP-based solution projecting its own assignments back into the load estimates to capture load coupling, and (iv) a facility mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler pricing the energy of batched requests collectively rather than in isolation. Across three LLMs under MLPerf SLOs and varying system loads, the MILP-based option offers the best carbon-SLO balance, reducing carbon emissions by up to 60% relative to the round-robin policy, with an average SLO violation of 3%. Our characterization further shows that savings grow with the spread of carbon intensity across datacenters and shrink as system load increases, while SLO attainment depends on how frequently schedulers receive datacenters' load updates.

title: DS and AMDS Symbol-Pair Codes from Three Families of Simple Root Cyclic Codes
abstract: Symbol-pair distances of simple-root cyclic codes are important for evaluating error correction performance under overlapping pair read channels. In this paper, we construct three families of simple-root cyclic codes over finite fields of odd characteristic via generator polynomials. For length \(2q+2\), the minimum symbol-pair distance is \(10\) for every odd prime power \(q\ge 7\), established by excluding invalid support configurations. For length \(4q-4\), when \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\) and finite field constraints hold, it is \(9\) or \(10\). For length \(2(q-1)\), reciprocal-polynomial analysis shows it is \(11\) or \(12\). All obtained codes are MDS or AMDS symbol-pair codes.

title: Data, programs and VIPR certificates for “The largest minimum distance of ternary LCD codes of dimensions four and five”
abstract: Data set (version 1.0.2) of the paper “The largest minimum distance of ternary LCD codes of dimensions four and five” by K. Promjiraprawat, W. Wongseree and D. Setsirichok. LCD_package_v1.0.2.zip holds the generator matrices of all codes, the programs, the integer-programming models, the solver logs, the result files and the LaTeX source of the paper; its README.md maps each statement of the paper to the files and the command that check it, and python3 src/verify_all.py re-checks the codes and the proofs’ counts and regenerates the paper’s tables. The other 35 files hold the VIPR certificates of infeasibility for the 73 integer programs of Section 6.4, produced by SCIP 10.1.0 with SoPlex 8.1.0 in exact mode and checked by viprchk: the zip archives LCD_vipr_certificates_v1.0.1_01.zip to _07.zip hold the 66 certificates of at most 200 MB, and the 7 larger ones are cut into pieces NAME.vipr.xz.partNN of 200,000,000 bytes. LCD_vipr_certificates_v1.0.1_contents.txt lists which certificate is in which file, with the SHA-256 and MD5 of every file. To use the certificates, download the files into one directory DIR, unpack the package and run python3 src/join_certificates.py DIR, which joins the pieces and checks every certificate against the SHA-256 recorded in results.jsonl.

title: Two-Stage Measurement of Update Adherence in Language Model Memory Agents: benchmark, event records, and scoring scripts
abstract: Benchmark scenarios, event records, frozen memory engine, and scoring scripts for the paper "Two-Stage Measurement of Update Adherence in Language Model Memory Agents". Update Adherence (UA) measures whether a revised requirement, and not the statement it replaced, governs the answer of a language model agent with external memory. It is scored at two stages with deterministic rules and no language-model judge, in the assembled context that the memory system hands to the answering model and in the generated answer. Every number in the paper can be recomputed from the files in this archive with python analysis/make_tables.py. Code is under the MIT License. Scenario data, result data, and figure data are under CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-DATA).

title: HEAIN-SD-1.0: การสรางคำบรรยายและการพากยเสยงภาษาไทยทกำกบดวยนโยบายบนโหนด Hybrid Edge AI
abstract: ระบบพากย์เสียงอัตโนมัติในปัจจุบันสร้างเสียงที่ฟังเข้าใจได้แล้ว แต่งานคำบรรยายและงานพากย์ระดับมืออาชีพยังติดปัญหาสามข้อที่ไม่ค่อยได้รับการแก้พร้อมกัน ข้อแรก อารมณ์ในการส่งเสียงต้องมีผู้ที่อ่านภาพเป็นผู้กำกับ ข้อสอง เนื้อหาที่มีคำหยาบหรือต้อง censor ต้องเป็นไปตามกฎที่ต่างกันตามประเทศและแพลตฟอร์มปลายทาง และข้อสาม การบันทึกเสียงที่ทำให้ระบบเก่งขึ้นเป็นข้อมูลส่วนบุคคลของเจ้าของเสียงที่ระบุตัวตนได้ บทความนี้เสนอ HEAIN-SD-1.0 ซึ่งเป็นโปรไฟล์ระดับแอปพลิเคชัน (Application Profile) ที่กำหนดว่าโมดูลสร้างคำบรรยายและพากย์เสียงที่เน้นภาษาไทยทำงานอย่างไรในฐานะ Layer 3 (Application AI) บน HEAIN Core Protocol และสถาปัตยกรรม Hybrid Edge AI Node บทความนำเสนอผลงานสี่ข้อ ข้อแรก บันไดความอัตโนมัติที่กำกับด้วยนโยบาย (L0–L3) ซึ่งระบบเรียนรู้ได้ทุกอย่างเกี่ยวกับการส่งเสียง แต่ไม่เรียนรู้ว่าอะไรอนุญาตให้พูด เพราะนโยบายเนื้อหาเป็นคลังที่มีเจ้าของแยกต่างหาก เลือกตามปลายทาง และ fail-closed ข้อสอง การแยกเสียงพากย์เป็นสี่ส่วน โดยเนื้อเสียงมาจากการแสดงต้นฉบับ สำเนียงมาจากมาตรฐานของทีมพากย์มืออาชีพในประเทศเป้าหมาย และอารมณ์กับจังหวะมาจากคำกำกับของโปรดิวเซอร์ ซึ่งทำได้ด้วยการสังเคราะห์เสียงที่ใช้ตัวอย่างซึ่งค้นมาเป็นพรอมต์จากคลังการส่งเสียงมืออาชีพที่ได้รับความยินยอม ข้อสาม โปรไฟล์โปรโตคอลที่มีแบบจำลอง session การแบ่งโซน CORE/EDGE และรายการขาขึ้นที่อนุญาต ซึ่งเก็บสื่อไว้ที่โหนดประมวลผล และส่งขึ้นโหนดควบคุมเฉพาะระเบียนข้อมูล คะแนน และ embedding ขนาดเล็ก ข้อสี่ แผนการประเมินผลที่กำหนดเกณฑ์ผ่านไว้ก่อนการทดลองใดๆ บทความนี้ไม่มีผลการทดลอง โปรไฟล์เป็นแบบที่ยังไม่ได้พัฒนาจริง และทุกปริมาณที่ระบุว่าเป็นค่าประมาณคือค่าที่ใช้วางแผน คำสำคัญ: Automatic Dubbing, Subtitling, ภาษาไทย, Voice Cloning, ภาษามีวรรณยุกต์, Human-in-the-Loop, นโยบายเนื้อหา, Edge Computing, การจัดการความยินยอม, ข้อกำหนดโปรโตคอล

title: AUŠRA: The Architectural Impact of Intuition, Instinct, and Quarantine on Decision Speed, Threat Detection, Authorization, and Survival A Synthetic Causal Exploration of the Integrated AUŠRA–EGIDA–LASO-Σ–KASK-Q–BITE Architecture
abstract: AUŠRA: Scientific Significance and Architectural Contribution Authors: Egidijus Kasiulevičius, Ąžuolas Kasiulevičius, Saulė Kasiulevičiūtė, Aušra KasiulevičienėDate: 10 October 2026 Summary AUŠRA is an integrated autonomous decision-making architecture designed to coordinate rapid response, information retrieval, conditional authorization, threat detection, quarantine, and adaptive feedback. The research investigates how adding INSTINCT, INTUITION, and QUARANTINE may change the behavior of the complete AUŠRA architecture, including EGIDA, LASO-Σ, KASK-Q, and BITE. The central principle is that improving an autonomous system does not necessarily mean increasing every performance metric simultaneously. Faster decisions may introduce risks; additional interpretation may improve threat detection while increasing decision time; and quarantine may reduce false actions while also suppressing relevant signals if its rules are too restrictive. AUŠRA therefore treats these mechanisms as complementary components whose individual effects and interactions must be evaluated together. Key significance to science 1. A system-level approach to autonomous decision-making The research emphasizes that decision speed, accuracy, authorization, and survival are interconnected properties of an architecture. A component's value cannot be established solely by measuring its isolated performance. 2. The coordination of fast response and controlled authorization INSTINCT represents a fast protective-response pathway, while LASO-Σ preserves conditional authorization. The architectural question is how to reduce dangerous delays without granting unrestricted authority to emergency actions. 3. The trade-off between threat detection and information quarantine INTUITION and QUARANTINE illustrate different potential trade-offs. Additional interpretation may improve detection at the cost of processing time, while excessive isolation may reduce false actions but increase missed threats. These effects require causal testing rather than assumptions about which component is beneficial. 4. A method for investigating component interactions The research proposes evaluating individual contributions, interactions, and full-system outcomes through matched scenarios, experimental ablations, independent repetitions, and uncertainty estimates. Modules are isolated for testing, not automatically removed from the architecture. 5. A measurable framework for safety-aware optimization The proposed evaluation combines decision steps, critical-threat detection, false-action rates, authorization violations, and safe outcomes before a deadline. This avoids declaring success based on speed alone. Preliminary results and scientific boundaries In the previously reported synthetic M6.9 model, the integrated AUŠRA configuration showed: Decision steps: 99.9 to 94.9. Critical-threat detection: 90.49% to 91.44%. False-action rate: 10.82% to 8.78%. Safe outcomes before the deadline: 42.07% to 50.88%. These are descriptive results from a synthetic exploratory model, not independently validated measurements of a deployed AUŠRA implementation. Statistical significance and real-world performance advantages have not yet been established. The current research status is M6.9 — PARTIAL PASS. Conclusion The principal scientific contribution is a testable architectural framework for investigating how rapid protective response, interpretation, information isolation, conditional authorization, structural information addressing, and adaptive feedback can be coordinated within one autonomous system. The research does not assume that every module improves every metric. Instead, it investigates the conditions under which each component contributes to the overall balance between speed, decision quality, authorization, and safety. The next scientific step is independent, reproducible causal evaluation of the integrated architecture. title: "DGRP-miniF2F-PISA-ControlBench"
abstract: "Beyond retrieving established facts, formal theorem proving often requires formulating auxiliary lemmas and coordinating their logical dependencies. We represent proof dependencies as an executable directed acyclic graph (DAG) and propose DGRP (DAG-Guided Recursive Prover). Within this graph, a language model generates auxiliary lemmas for recursive decomposition or synthesizes direct formal proof scripts. To reuse decomposition patterns across theorems, DGRP maintains a persistent decomposition memory of local decomposition records checked in their source theory contexts and retrieves them to guide auxiliary lemma generation for subsequent theorems. We evaluate DGRP on miniF2F, a continuous mathematics subset extracted via PISA, and our designed ControlBench. On miniF2F with Gemini 3.1 Pro, combining DAG structuring with recursive refinement raises the pass@3 verification rate from 38.1\\% for a direct formal prover to 69.7\\% for DGRP without decomposition memory. Across evaluated settings, decomposition memory provides an additional improvement of up to 4.7 percentage points. These results provide empirical evidence that explicitly organizing proof dependencies and reusing decomposition patterns can improve automated formal reasoning."

title: BrainAid: Efficient Brain Tumor Detection Using Lightweight CNNs and Explainable AI for Resource-Constrained Environments
abstract: A brain tumor is an unusual growth of cells in the brain that can be cancerous or not, affecting normal brain function and causing serious risk to health. Existing solutions for brain tumor classification, such as expert manual evaluations of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, are generally inconsistent as different professionals have different criteria and can be resource-intensive, leading to delayed diagnoses. Additionally, while deep learning models have demonstrated potential, they typically require significant computational resources, motivating the need for more efficient and accessible diagnostic tools that can be deployed in real-time healthcare settings. To address these limitations, this study presents BrainAid, which makes efficient use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) for effective classification of four-class classification of glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no-tumor MRI scans, outperforming all the standard models such as VGG16, Inception-V3, ResNet-50 and so, while integrating Explainable AI (XAI) to improve interpretability. The BrainAid is trained to classify tumors with a high precision of 98%, achieving an F1 score of 98% and an accuracy of 98% using publicly available dataset. The model is deployed on a Raspberry Pi, demonstrating efficiency in low-resource environments. This system shows the feasibility of real-time, edge-based tumor classification, providing quick diagnostic support for medical professionals and enhancing patient care in resource-limited healthcare facilities and underserved areas.

title: Explore This! Beat and Downbeat Tracking From a Learned Tatum Grid
abstract: State-of-the-art beat tracking is based on neural networks that model beats and downbeats as individual events, often followed by a separate Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) enforcing musical consistency. We propose a novel architecture that combines deep learning with differentiable theory-based modules: Specifically, we design a system that first predicts a tatum grid, then groups tatum events to beats and downbeats, explicitly modelling multiple options for the current tempo and time signature in a bar-pointer-like fashion. Our approach improves continuity metrics compared to existing DBN-free systems and is more versatile than the de-facto standard DBN, but still falls behind the best DBN-based methods on average. Given the many design choices and hyperparameters involved, we assume we have not yet explored the full potential of this idea and publish our code and invite others to explore this further.

title: Enhancing Knowledge Management in Green Building Engineering: A Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation Approach to Support Project Assessment
abstract: Abstract Green building assessment relies heavily on manual queries of complex engineering regulations, making the introduction of knowledge management theories crucial for improving assessment efficiency. However, the inherent characteristics of engineering regulations—dense terminology, complex clause dependencies, and frequent revisions—limit the effectiveness of traditional knowledge engineering. This study aims to explore the utilization of advanced information technologies to achieve reliable knowledge management for supporting engineering decision-making. From the perspective of acquisition, organization, retrieval, and presentation (AORP), a domain knowledge management framework is designed by integrating network analysis, information retrieval, and large language models (LLMs) with traditional knowledge management theories. A dual-structure knowledge network is proposed as the underlying carrier to characterize explicit rules and semantic dependencies, enabling lightweight knowledge organization. Furthermore, a hybrid retrieval algorithm capable of identifying and adaptively weighting domain terms was developed and embedded into a retrieval-augmented generation workflow. Facilitated by LLMs, the proposed framework supports more efficient, traceable, and scalable building assessment. This study covers regulations containing 225,604 words and validates the effectiveness of the proposed method using 132 practical test cases. The results showed that the proposed method achieves a recall rate of 0.959, effectively reduces generation hallucinations, and substantially improves the accuracy and reliability of knowledge presentation. More importantly, the experiments indicated that the performance gap among LLMs with different parameter scales narrowed after introducing domain knowledge, confirming that an effective knowledge management architecture in vertical domains has the potential to reduce dependence on large-parameter LLMs and provide a feasible pathway for low-cost deployment of intelligent applications in the industry.

The results showed that the proposed method achieves a recall rate of 0.959, effectively reduces generation hallucinations, and substantially improves the accuracy and reliability of knowledge presentation. More importantly, the experiments indicated that the performance gap among LLMs with different parameter scales narrowed after introducing domain knowledge, confirming that an effective knowledge management architecture in vertical domains has the potential to reduce dependence on large-parameter LLMs and provide a feasible pathway for low-cost deployment of intelligent applications in the industry.

title: Generative learning of time series with holographic quantum circuit sampling
abstract: Quantum generative models face growing qubit requirements and concentrated loss landscapes when learning long time series. Here we introduce holographic quantum circuit sampling (HQCS), which combines mid-circuit measurements, qubit reuse and independently parameterized temporal blocks to generate trajectories with a fixed number of qubits. For Haar-random HQCS and a normalized exponential kernel, we prove inverse-polynomial bounds on maximum mean discrepancy loss variance, contrasting with exponential concentration in global Haar-random generators. For generic members of a family of nonstationary Markov processes, temporal parameterization reduces exact-generation gate counts from quadratic to linear in sequence length relative to a specified class of repeated shared-block generators. Simulations demonstrate learning of Gaussian autoregressive processes and historical Volatility Index (VIX) trajectories, with the latter achieving over tenfold lower maximum mean discrepancy than the tested classical benchmarks. These results establish a framework for quantum time-series generation with fixed qubit requirements and provable avoidance of exponential loss concentration as sequence length grows.

title: Internal Languages for Thin Epsilon-Hyperdoctrines: Soundness, Completeness, and Rocq Formalization
abstract: We present a typed proof-term calculus for intuitionistic intensional first-order logic with Hilbert's epsilon-operator and prove its soundness and completeness with respect to hyperdoctrinal models with thin bicartesian closed setoid categories (BiCCCs) as fibres and formula-indexed witness selections. The calculus provides an explicit internal language for these epsilon-hyperdoctrines: for each fixed typed signature, its syntactic term model is initial for syntax-indexed, interpretation-preserving model morphisms, with uniqueness up to setoid equality. The nested epsilon syntax is organized by a well-founded dependency relation on formula labels. Concrete countermodels exhibit failure of excluded middle and show that formula conversion need not identify the selected witnesses. We also compare the full calculus with its epsilon-free and epsilon-only fragments. The principal constructions and metatheorems are formalized in Rocq. With setoid BiCCCs, proof irrelevance is a choice of equality, not the erasure of proofs: the proofs and their categorical operations remain available as the basis for a future proof-relevant categorical semantics.

title: Toward a Multimodal Foundation Model for Plasma State Reconstruction
abstract: Plasma experiments observe coupled physical states through sparse, heterogeneous, and incomplete diagnostics. We present a proof of concept toward a multimodal foundation model for plasma state reconstruction during magnetic reconnection, motivated by the Facility for Laboratory Reconnection Experiments (FLARE). Using 250 synthetic VPIC simulations at fixed reference electron beta $β_{e0}=0.2$, with 225 training runs and 25 disjoint validation runs, we train a 5.5M-parameter residual 3D U-Net to reconstruct three magnetic-field components and electron density from incomplete observations. The model combines spatial-only pooling, which preserves all 24 temporal frames, with global spatiotemporal self-attention and rotary positional encoding. Independently masking magnetic and density modalities across random, grid, block, and temporal patterns enables sparse sensing, cross-modal completion, density super-resolution, and temporal completion with a single set of weights and no task-specific retraining. With density fully hidden, just 0.1% magnetic spatial visibility reduces median density NRMSE from approximately 0.9 to 0.1. Conversely, observed density improves current-density reconstruction when magnetic data are absent or extremely sparse. With no magnetic observations, roughly 1% density visibility approaches the density reconstruction accuracy achieved with fully observed magnetic fields, although current structure remains more dependent on direct magnetic measurements. Full magnetic conditioning also stabilizes completion of missing future density frames. These results demonstrate bidirectional cross-modal predictive coupling within this simulation regime. Generalization across plasma regimes or to experimental measurements remains untested.

title: Seamless Deployment of Machine Learning Inference at the Far Edge: An Empirical AWS IoT Greengrass Architecture for Industrial Predictive Maintenance
abstract: Industrial IoT sensors produce continuous, high-volume data streams that predictive maintenance needs to analyse in real time. Cloud-centric architectures send all raw telemetry to central servers, which costs latency, bandwidth and resilience. This paper presents a hybrid cloud-edge architecture for manufacturing predictive maintenance built on AWS IoT Core and AWS IoT Greengrass v2, with local machine learning inference at the edge and selective cloud synchronization. We deploy two configurations on real AWS infrastructure and compare them: a cloud-only baseline (Configuration A) and the proposed hybrid edge architecture (Configuration B). We measure end-to-end inference latency, bandwidth consumption and inference accuracy. Configuration B cuts cloud-bound bandwidth by 86.8% (63.6 KB to 7.2 KB per 200-reading window) and decision latency by 256x (23.1 ms cloud round trip to 0.09 ms local inference). At the edge, with no cloud involvement, it keeps an anomaly-class F1 score of 0.84 and 91% recall. The evaluation also instruments system uptime and Stream Manager queuing under cloud disconnection; the quantitative disconnection experiment is left as planned work. Our review of the literature points to four gaps that this work addresses: the lack of empirically validated Greengrass v2 deployments for predictive maintenance, unquantified bandwidth savings from selective edge synchronization, unmeasured resilience under cloud disconnection, and the open MLOps feedback loop at the edge.

title: FrameFold: Response-Guided KV Cache Consolidation for Autoregressive Long Video Generation
abstract: In autoregressive video generation, retaining all historical key-value (KV) states increases memory usage and per-step attention costs as videos grow longer. A fixed cache budget bounds these costs but raises the challenge of preserving historical content that supports consistent, high-quality generation. Existing methods control cache size through history selection or consolidation, yet deciding what to retain and how to limit the loss of useful content remains a shared challenge. Our analysis shows that spatial queries depend on different historical content and that higher current attention coverage does not necessarily yield better long-video quality. We introduce FrameFold, a training-free KV cache consolidation method that compares the content retrieved by the same recent historical queries before and after merging to guide both representative construction and merge selection. Exploiting temporal redundancy between adjacent historical entries, FrameFold merges their KV states into shared representatives while retaining complete spatial grids. It fits value-merging coefficients in closed form by matching conditional attention responses, then selects the merge with the lowest remaining response distortion. Under matched KV cache budgets, experiments on Self Forcing and Causal Forcing at 30 and 60 seconds and on LongLive at 120 seconds demonstrate improved consistency and visual quality. Continuous eight-minute Self Forcing rollouts further show less quality degradation than the baselines.

title: Who Carries the Context? Recovery and User Re-Provision in MemUse
abstract: This qualitative secondary analysis of 72 selected MemUse target rows identifies two initial focal earlier-session recoveries (pos_031, pos_073), one delayed partial focal recovery (pos_020), three ancillary earlier-session recovery observations (pos_041, pos_044, pos_062), and one High current-session reference resolution (pos_019). These are case observations, not a success rate. Most focal targets cannot independently test recovery under this framework: 66 rows receive “Not testable.” Three observed material corrections concern current-session interpretation; two concern earlier-state restoration, both after technical interruption. There are zero verified unconfounded earlier-state repair messages in the coded windows. The corpus therefore supports distinctions among recovery, user-supplied continuity and observable restoration, but does not establish a causal recovery–burden relationship or cumulative long-horizon collaboration. This secondary question differs from MemUse’s natural-integration objective. AI-assisted qualitative secondary analysis. Coding and audits by the same assistant; no independent reliability or peer review. Supplement includes a 72-row current register, codebook, review record and reproducible structural source checks. No full source conversations or internal drafts. Source: MemUse by Ryuichi Sumida, Koji Inoue and Tatsuya Kawahara (2026), https://huggingface.co/datasets/RuiSumida/memuse. Source data and this source-derived analysis: CC BY-NC 4.0. New annotations and interpretations; no endorsement implied.

title: Source Code and Evaluation Data for Adaptive MPC Safety Shield in Microrobot Navigation
abstract: This repository contains the complete source code, configuration files, and raw evaluation data associated with the study on microrobot navigation. abstract: This archive contains the independent formal verification vault and forensic validation receipts for the complete OAI.NumberTheory.PiExponent subtree (869 modules) within the OpenAI mathematics catalogue (Family 017: the irrationality exponent of pi). title: Fleet Transfer: Cross-Robot Learning from Nineteen-Number Events, with a Corrected Physical Validation
abstract: The fifth paper in this series, PAV, proposed that robots could share physical knowledge by exchanging compact, 19-number routing events instead of raw trajectories, and claimed the first physical-world validation of divergence-based violation detection. This paper does four things. First, it corrects PAV. A code-level audit found the published experiments never actually changed the simulated physics. With that fixed, the underlying mechanism performs better than originally claimed: 100% detection, 99.4% ± 1.2% divergence reduction across five seeds. Second, it validates the fleet-transfer claim for the first time. A robot that has never encountered ice correctly detects it after receiving nothing but 570 numbers from a robot that has, and recovers the identical 99.4% ± 1.2% divergence reduction. Transferred knowledge performs as well as knowledge earned directly. Third, it honestly maps where detection currently ends. An out-of-distribution guard’s blind band and a class-capture failure mode are both measured and quantified, not glossed over. Fourth, it reports a same-day follow-up that partially, not fully, closes both of those open problems. All experiments run on a consumer laptop CPU. Code, per-window records, and full result files are public.

title: Global Disaster Risk Assessment Using World Risk Index Data: A Geospatial and Visual Analytics Approach
abstract: The world has seen several threats that include resource depletion, food security, poverty and inequality, difficulties associated with urbanization, migration, and environmental effects. The World Risk Index (WRI) is a metric that is used to measure the susceptibility of nations against natural disasters and related risks that is reported by the Humanitarian Data Exchange. The WRI is comprised of factors such as susceptibility, vulnerability to natural hazards, and coping mechanisms. The WRI index has allowed to recognize regions in advance in order to face threats and situations beforehand. This study was conducted by analyzing the data that was related to years from 2000 to 2025 using data visualization techniques. Python related libraries of Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Geopandas were used due to their efficiency and usability in analyzing WRI data. As per the analysis, it was identified that countries of Philippines, Mexico, Indonesia, and India were recorded with high WRI index values that showed these nations should be prepared for natural disasters and situations. Hence, this study has provided insights using data visualization techniques in understanding natural disasters and threats so that necessary measures can be taken

title: Almost every Boolean function has central threshold degree
abstract: The polynomial threshold degree (or threshold degree) of a Boolean function is the least degree of a real polynomial whose sign represents it. We prove that almost every Boolean function has polynomial threshold degree among the central one or two integers. More precisely, a uniformly chosen Boolean function on $n$ variables has threshold degree $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ or $\lceil n/2\rceil$ except with probability at most $\exp(-c2^{n/2}/n)$, for an absolute constant $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. A parity example gives a lower bound on the exceptional probability whose exponent differs from ours by a factor of order $n$. The proof relates polynomial sign representation to recovery of Reed--Muller codes from random erasures, and combines sharp-threshold estimates with bounds on generalized Hamming weights and minimum distance.

title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Dengue Infection Using Clinical and Hematological Data from Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Benchmark and Extended Prediction Models
abstract: Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV) and a major public health concern in Bangladesh, where symptom overlap with other febrile illnesses complicates early diagnosis. This study compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost to predict dengue from clinical and hematological data using two Bangladeshi hospital datasets (2024, n=1,511; 2025, n=1,283) with SMOTE. Extended models outperformed benchmarks within 2024 (Random Forest ROC-AUC 0.640 to 0.661), with RDW-CV the most consistently influential added predictor. 2025 benchmark performance was higher (ROC-AUC 0.904), unexplained by class imbalance and possibly reflecting data quality. External validation is needed.

title: Blind by Design: Numerical checks and simulations for 'Quantum Error Correction, Functional Incompatibility and the Value of Evidence'
abstract: Supplementary code for Peter Kahl, ‘Blind by Design: Quantum Error Correction, Functional Incompatibility and the Value of Evidence’ (Lex et Ratio Working Paper LXR-2026-PHI-BBDQEC-WP, Version 1.0, 2026, doi: 10.5281/zenodo.23278643). Five Python scripts reproduce every computational result in the paper, and each comes with the complete console output of its reference run. prop52_numerical_check.py checks Proposition 5.2, which bounds how much a quantum error-correction record can reveal about the stored state by how far the process is from being undoable. The check uses the toric-code instrument of Özgüler (2026) and a three-qubit repetition code. The script also compares what the process passes to its environment with what the classical record keeps. It then brackets, by semidefinite programming, the best repair available to a controller that does or does not know the sign of a coherent error, with the syndrome history discarded or used. blind_by_design_toy_repetition_code.py gives the minimal example of a record blind both to the stored state and to the sign of the noise. ozguler_prop1_check.py independently checks the result of Özgüler (2026) on which the paper relies. audit_checks.pyaudits the construction of the surface-code simulations (Appendix A). blind_by_design_continuous_misspecification.py shows a decoder’s wrong model detected and repaired from its own records. Every reported bound is a floating-point construction made independent of the solver’s tolerance. None is interval-certified. The reference runs used Python 3.12.3. All five scripts were also rerun on macOS with Python 3.14.7: three reproduced exactly, one differed only at rounding level, and the semidefinite-programming check differed only in the solver’s last digits, with all checks passing. Includes a reliance note on Özgüler (2026). MIT Licence.

title: Ensemble Voting of Large Language Models for Multiple-Choice Answer Prediction
abstract: Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) has become a key benchmark for evaluating natural language processing systems, and multiple-choice question answering is widely adopted for assessing reasoning, comprehension, and commonsense inference capabilities. However, traditional embedding-based retrieval models often struggle with complex reasoning and lack sufficient external knowledge. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong language understanding and reasoning abilities, relying on a single model remains challenging due to hallucinations, model biases, and differences in training data, architectures, and domain expertise. As a result, no individual model can consistently achieve optimal performance across diverse multiple-choice question answering tasks. To address these limitations, we propose an ensemble framework for multiple-choice question answering. The framework incorporates a novel model selection mechanism that identifies model combinations with minimal error overlap, thereby maximizing error-correction capability. In addition, when disagreements occur among base models, a Thinking Model is dynamically invoked to analyze and resolve conflicting predictions, enabling advanced reasoning only when necessary. Experimental results show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms individual models across multiple datasets and previous ensemble approaches. At the same time, it significantly reduces inference time and computational cost compared to the strongest benchmark models.

title: Exposing AI Inference as a Telco Network API over the 5G User Plane
abstract: Supporting edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference as a network service is challenging because current mobile systems can transport tensors but do not expose or understand the inference context that gives those tensors operational meaning. Prior studies have addressed this gap through dynamic partitioning, collaborative inference, and split pipelines; however, these solutions remain application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. This work proposes Inference on Demand (IoD), an inference-on-demand abstraction that exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like Application Program Interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band across the 5G user plane path. We evaluate the IoD on a programmable user plane function (UPF)-based testbed using a partitionable visual AI workload, showing that adaptive split selection can operate as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static configurations. Including our findings, split inference becomes more than offloading when the service intent, runtime partitioning, and tensor transport are made visible to the mobile data plane. This opens a path toward network-native AI services, in which programmable telco infrastructure coordinates computation, context, and connectivity for user-facing applications.

title: Depth-progressive 3D seismic velocity model building via 2D generative diffusion models
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) velocity model building (VMB) remains computationally challenging with conventional approaches and native 3D neural networks, largely due to the prohibitive memory and training cost of full 3D formulations. Therefore, we introduce a depth-progressive framework that achieves 3D VMB using 2D generative diffusion models through a depth-as-channel formulation, in which the depth dimension of each 3D velocity patch is mapped to the channel dimension of a 2D U-Net. This allows the model to synthesize overlapping depth patches sequentially from shallow to deep while conditioning the prediction of the deeper patch on the shallower one, as well as on any available geophysical constraints, including well logs and structural attributes. During training, paired shallow-deep patch pairs with randomized overlaps are used to teach the network how deeper velocity structures relate to shallower information, and a classifier-free guidance strategy enables the model to handle missing constraints gracefully. At inference, starting from a shallow velocity prior, the model recursively generates deeper patches in a top-down manner, and a depth-attenuated Gaussian blending scheme merges overlapping predictions into spatially coherent 3D volumes while accounting for the progressive accumulation of uncertainty at greater depths. Numerical experiments on both in-distribution benchmark models, including Overthrust, SEAM Arid, and SEG/EAGE, and the out-of-distribution Marmousi model demonstrate that the method effectively propagates shallow velocity priors downward and produces high-quality 3D velocity volumes across a range of geological settings and conditioning scenarios. Compared to a 3D benchmark of equivalent architecture, the proposed method significantly reduces parameter count, training cost, and inference cost, while maintaining superior VMB accuracy.

title: The Grounding Tax: How Domain Fine-Tuning Suppresses Context Utilisation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are routinely adapted to specialised domains through fine-tuning and grounded in external evidence through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The prevailing assumption is that these methods are complementary even though minimal empirical work examines whether domain-specific fine-tuning influences a model’s responsiveness to retrieved context. Thus, this study examines the interaction between fine-tuning and RAG through a controlled evaluation in a high-stakes public-finance domain. The evaluation is conducted through 12 model configurations built on two open-weight model families (LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B), using a frozen 100-query benchmark covering factual question-answering (factual-QA), risk assessment, and summarisation under both closed-book and context-matched conditions. The evidence confirms successful knowledge injection as domain fine-tuning raised closed-book numeric-fact accuracy (NFA) from 0.148 to 0.248. However, when retrieved context is introduced, the benefit collapses as the base model gained +0.183 from context while the fine-tuned model gained only +0.021. Across the backbone pairs, the change in context gain ranged from -0.161 to -0.348 and was statistically significant for the LLaMA Instruct and Qwen Base pairs. Further ablation analysis shows that prompt-template and instruction alignment can amplify this effect. We term this phenomenon the grounding tax: domain fine-tuning imposes a measurable cost on the model’s ability to use retrieved evidence because the adapted model relies on internally encoded knowledge rather than faithfully using the evidence supplied to it. Thus, these findings show that conventional closed-book evaluation can mask degradation in context utilisation and that fine-tuned RAG systems must be evaluated jointly under both closed-book and context-conditioned settings. Therefore, we argue for treating domain adaptation, instruction alignment, and retrieval grounding as distinct and potentially competing design dimensions.

title: Mechanism-Attribution Audit for Clinical Prediction — Replication Package
abstract: Replication package for Rahman Ifti and Mukherjee, "Mechanism Attribution for Subgroup Error-Rate Disparities in Clinical Classifiers: A Design-Aware Audit Protocol, Demonstrated on Cross-Sectional Hypertension Detection" (manuscript in preparation). Version 2.0.0 corrects errors found in a full re-audit of version 1.0.0. The results in version 1.0.0 should not be used. Adults with no blood pressure reading are now excluded from the NHANES cohort (N = 19,311). The survey bootstrap now uses the Rao-Wu rescaling. The prevalence-matching test (T2) now refits the model, because resampling the test set cannot change a false negative rate. MIMIC-IV intervals now use Newcombe score intervals and Fisher's exact test, which stay valid when a subgroup has no detected deaths. The feature-by-race interaction analysis now uses a reference model that includes race, and an undocumented clustered simulation is replaced by a scripted one. README.md lists every change. Contents: analysis code for the NHANES and MIMIC-IV arms, the aggregate result files behind every table and figure, Figures 1-4, and the manuscript with the script that builds it from those files. No record-level data is included. NHANES public-use files are available from the CDC, and MIMIC-IV requires PhysioNet credentialing.

title: Towards Reliable Prosody Detection in Teaching Practical Phonetics: A Sustainable Digital Approach
abstract: This research focuses on providing quality education to specialists in the field of linguistic studies, phonology, theoretical and practical phonetics by creating an innovative automated service which can ease the linguists endeavour to transcribe and examine suprasegmental features of human speech prosody. The authors attempted to design a docker-based architecture for prosody labelling. The pre-processing stage compiled 47 manually marked recordings, ten of which were annotated at clip level. The data-processing stage produced a corpus of 882 denoised, labelled clips via librosa , noisereduce , and Label Studio. The model selection stage compared 4909 scikit-learn configurations and 120 CNN configurations. The strongest classical approach (Random Forest) achieved an accuracy of 0.373, whereas the best CNN scored 0.455 against a majority-class baseline of 0.316. Per-class analysis showed that the classical models performed poorly across most intonation categories, assigning 94% of predictions to the two most frequent classes. These results indicate early-stage prototype performance rather than a validated evaluation and are not yet sufficient to support reliable automatic intonation marking. Having recognised the prototype limitations, the researchers have scheduled a roadmap for improving the tool. The suggested model applies the principles of machine learning to automatically generate prosodic analysis that extends beyond individual sound segments and reflects suprasegmental aspects of prosody including rhythm, intonation, and phrasal stress.

title: Deep Learning-based Semantic Segmentation of Dental Radiographs: Comparative Evaluation of PSPNet, DeepLabv3, UNet, and UNet++
abstract: Accurate and efficient analysis of dental radiographs has become increasingly important for disease diagnosis and clinical decision making. In particular, dental radiographs segmentation plays a critical role as it is challenging due to several reasons, such as low contrast, noise in the images, variations in the image quality, etc. Previous studies have primarily addressed these challenges using convolutional neural networks (CNN)-based models. However, direct comparison of these segmentation models is still challenging due to the variations among the experimental settings. Therefore, we mainly compared four segmentation models, including Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet), DeepLabV3, UNet, and UNet++, through a fair, controlled experimentation setting under varying conditions such as image sizes and batch sizes. For this, we used 1269 dental radiography images, and prior to training, we implemented a series of preprocessing techniques. To assess the models, we used several metrics, including Dice coefficient (DICE), Intersection over Union (IoU), accuracy, precision, training and validation losses. According to our results, UNet++ demonstrated the highest IoU score of 0.6719, and a DICE value of 0.7869, showing superior results in terms of segmentation, specifically when configured with an image size of 300x300 and a batch size of 16. In addition, we also explored the effect of image resolutions and batch sizes on model performance and accuracy under different architectures. Therefore, this study provides insights into the strengths of different segmentation models and the potential of deep learning-based semantic segmentation methods for improving automated dental radiograph analysis.

title: KedgeFlow: A Programmable Control Plane for Enterprise AI Agents
abstract: Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, concurrently reuse the same permission, or retry operations whose responses were lost. These failures arise when approval and resource execution lack a shared contract. KedgeFlow specifies language-independent contracts for trusted controllers to authorize state-changing operations and privileged gateways to enforce that authority independently of agent reasoning. Inspired by OpenFlow, it connects policy checks supported by evidence, signed permission for an exact action, a shared allowance that can be consumed only once, target-side conditions for applying the change, and retained outcome records. Under trusted issuance of exact-action authority, two conditional properties establish at most one successful claim per allowance and link every governed dispatch to a matching grant, claim, and subsequent dispatch authorization, even when the agent is compromised. A reference implementation exposes this execution path to agent systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In the single-resource evaluation, 6,560 concurrent ledger claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances. Boundary tests rejected unauthorized and altered requests before consumption. A 32-call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authorized an undesirable effect, exposing the limits of execution authorization. Evaluation uses three members of the etcd coordinated key-value store on one host, synthetic authentication and authorization inputs, and a mock target that rejects stale requests. Distributed reservations, enforcement of every production access route, native crash recovery, exactly-once effects at real targets, and interoperability between independent implementations remain untested.

title: Gradient reach in recurrent networks: code and training runs (LSTM, GRU, dropout, zoneout, chrono initialisation)
abstract: Code and complete results of 1299 training runs of one-layer LSTM and GRU networks on the adding problem and delayed recall, crossing gate initialisation (conventional, chrono) with six recurrent regulariser placements (per-step and variational dropout on the recurrent input, dropout on the candidate update, zoneout of the cell, hidden or both states). It accompanies the preprint "Gate Initialisation Outweighs Recurrent Regularisation in Gradient Propagation and in Learning Long Dependencies". For every run the archive contains the validation history, task-specific gradient probes and the input sensitivity of the final hidden state at every lag, measured at six checkpoints in evaluation and training mode. Every run is determined by its seed and can be repeated exactly with "cargo run --release -- run "; all tables and figures of the paper are regenerated with "python -m analysis results". Networks were trained with rust-lstm 0.10.0. Files: rnn-gradient-reach-1.0.0-code.zip (git tag v1.0.0, commit e4274d1); rnn-gradient-reach-1.0.0-results.tar.gz (runs.csv, history.csv, probes.csv and per-run gradient curves for the plans calibrate, calibrate_long, main, more_seeds, long_budget and chrono_mismatch); SHA256SUMS.

title: Data for "Multi-agent discovery of finite-length quantum LDPC codes"
abstract: This dataset accompanies the paper "Multi-agent discovery of finite-length quantum LDPC codes" by Dongheng Qian and Tianyi Li. It contains the code instances, distance evidence, literature benchmark and numerical data behind the reported results. - 01_code_instances: parity-check matrices (NumPy .npz and Matrix Market .mtx), parameters and constructions of the 36 reported CSS codes (the 7 codes of Table 1 and the 29 codes of Extended Data Table 1). - 02_distance_evidence: evidence for every reported distance. 21 exact distances are certified by mixed-integer linear programming (8 with all subproblems solved, 13 with subproblems reduced by code symmetries), with solver logs and records, logical bases and symmetry certificates; 15 upper bounds are given by explicit logical operators. - 03_literature_benchmark: the literature benchmark dataset of 1,354 code records from 93 references, in two linked CSV files. - 04_figure_source_data: numerical source data for Figs. 2 and 3 and Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2. - 05_decoding_data: code-capacity Monte Carlo counts for 13 codes, and circuit-level counts together with the 28 Stim circuits, syndrome-extraction schedules, logical bases and simulation settings used to obtain them. README.md gives an overview, and DATA_DICTIONARY.md defines every file and variable and links it to the tables and figures of the paper.

Version 0.1.0 provides a verified Cantor-normal-form notation system whose canonical terms represent exactly the ordinals below ε₀, together with executable comparison, semantic certification, mathlib ONote/NONote interoperability, and notation-level ordinal arithmetic.

title: Groups Don't Move as One: A Bregman Clustering View of Linearized Group Influence
abstract: Influence functions provide an efficient alternative to retraining for assessing the effects of removing or reweighting training data. For groups, however, the standard first-order estimate reduces individual contributions to a sum that can conceal substantial differences among members, including opposing effects that cancel. We establish a Bregman centroid formulation of the linearized group influence objective, interpreting this aggregate as a single representative and using Bregman information (BI) to quantify the variation it omits. Extending this formulation to multiple clusters reveals distinct contributions whose sum recovers the original estimate. We further propose an estimator that jointly optimizes the weights of these cluster contributions, rather than simply summing them. Experiments uncover cluster-specific influence patterns and a positive association between target-specific BI and approximation error. The proposed estimator achieves higher $R^2$ than standard group influence in predicting target changes under the nonlinear proximal Bregman response function. Simplified clustering and correction variants reduce computational cost. The centroid view thus explains what additive group influence leaves out and provides a basis for using that information to improve estimation.

title: AnyRank: Reliable Anytime Policy Ranking via Sequential Testing
abstract: Due to the high cost of hardware experiments, robot policies are predominantly evaluated by comparing their empirical performance on a limited number of hardware trials. However, finite-sample statistical uncertainty can lead to erroneous conclusions, especially when ranking multiple policies using a fixed batch of evaluation data. We propose AnyRank: a sequential method for multi-policy ranking that (i) adaptively allocates trials to hard-to-separate policies, (ii) provides (partial) rankings at any stopping time while bounding the probability of an incorrect ranking, and (iii) optionally exploits prior information to prioritize hardware evaluations more efficiently. This prior information could be informed from expert intuition, a small set of held-out hardware evaluations, or from policy rollouts in a simulator or an action-conditioned video world model. Notably, the prior can be imperfect; while a strong prior can provide efficiency gains on hardware, any inaccuracies in prior policy rankings do not invalidate the statistical assurances of AnyRank. We achieve the aforementioned properties through novel theoretical contributions that combine sequential testing with multiple-hypothesis graphical testing approaches. Experiments in simulation and real-world policy evaluation benchmarks show that AnyRank requires up to 50% fewer hardware evaluations compared to existing statistically rigorous approaches, while guarding against the incorrect rankings produced by heuristic methods used by state-of-the-art benchmarks.

title: CPT v4.4: Generative Cognitive Asset Identification and Formation Provenance - A Minimum Extension Claim
abstract: Abstract This note proposes two bounded conceptual extensions within the Cognitive Property Theory (CPT) research program: generative cognitive asset identification and formation provenance. The first addresses a distinction between a cognitive structure's generative function and its status as an identifiable cognitive asset. A structure may contribute to subsequent cognition without necessarily constituting a sufficiently identifiable, traceable, and reusable asset. Generative contribution alone therefore does not establish asset identity. The second addresses how the formation and transformation of a cognitive structure can be reconstructed while distinguishing contemporaneous records, subsequently verifiable evidence, retrospective interpretation, and causal inference. This evidentiary distinction is proposed as a refinement of existing work on Cognitive Provenance, not as a replacement for it. The note provisionally defines a generative cognitive asset as an identifiable and traceable cognitive structure whose reusable organization is supported by evidence of its contribution to the formation of further cognition across relevant contexts. Formation provenance refers to the evidence-oriented reconstruction of how a cognitive structure emerged and changed, including the sources, limitations, and inferential status of the evidence used. Longitudinal cognitive trajectories—including possible persistence, latency, reactivation, and transformation—are treated as a relevant research dimension within the existing accounts of Cognitive Formation and Evolution (CFE) and Generative Cognitive Dynamics (GCD), rather than as an independently claimed theoretical contribution of this note. These proposals refine the interfaces among cognitive formation, recursive generation, asset identification, continuity, and provenance. They remain provisional analytical distinctions requiring further literature comparison, operational specification, and empirical examination. This note does not claim that the underlying phenomena are unprecedented, that the proposed criteria have been validated, or that conceptual publication establishes exclusive legal rights over general cognitive mechanisms.

title: lean-pkg: a registry and trust gate for Lean 4 formalization packages
abstract: Added comparator-receipt --unit-size K (env LEAN_PKG_COMPARATOR_UNIT_SIZE) decouples the judge unit size from concurrency: each configuration's pending slots are cut into contiguous units of at most K names, and --judges N is then only how many units run at once (default 1). --unit-size 1 --judges 1 judges each name alone, one at a time, with every accepted slot cached at once, so a capped run resumes exactly where it stopped. Without --unit-size, --judges N behaves as before. The runner prints units: M of at most K names, width N once; the receipt and stages.json gain the additive unit_size (K or null) beside judges; a value that is not a positive integer exits 2, and the legacy mechanism refuses the flag. (#60) Changed comparator-receipt --estimate: the sample has a floor of max(5, ceil(0.25 * slots)) (capped at the slot count), which is also the default --sample; a smaller --sample or --slots subset is refused (exit 2, nothing written) unless --force-sample. recommended_cap uses the per-slot max model (per_slot_max_seconds * slots / judges) instead of the mean when the sample covers less than half the slots. The estimate JSON is schema comparator-estimate/2. A field run had capped a 16-slot configuration at 3000 s from a sample of 2; the unsampled 14-name unit outran it. (#59) Added comparator-receipt --estimate samples the heaviest slots first: each slot is weighted by the size of the olean of the module its name's longest namespace prefix names (0 when none matches), and the max(1, ceil(0.2 * K)) heaviest are taken before the namespace-stratified fill. The estimate gains estimated_seconds_max, cap_model (max or mean), sample_floor, sample_forced, per-row weight_bytes, weight_module and heavy, and a whole_unit_warning (a unit's export pays its names' union closure, which isolated timings do not bound; per-name units with --unit-size keep the model valid and the run resumable). --force-sample accepts a sample below the floor with a warning. docs/comparator.md documents the floor, the weight rule, both cap models and the warning. (#59) Fixed comparator --check (and gate --comparator, index add/index check, which share the validation) no longer refuses a receipt the runner wrote from a configuration that omits definition_names: a list field missing (or null) in the committed configuration now means [] on the check side too, as the runner records it, so the receipt definition_names differs from the config ([] vs None) refusal is gone; a real difference (["a"] vs []) is still refused. The runner names a missing permitted_axioms up front instead of calling it "not a list of strings". docs/comparator.md says which list fields may be omitted. (#61) comparator-receipt (toolchain mechanism) on a project without Mathlib no longer fails as lake comparator did not accept the solution: the vendored verify-comparator.sh ran lake exe cache get, which fails there with unknown executable cache. The runner refuses such a project before any stage with the toolchain mechanism needs a Mathlib dependency (lake-manifest.json has none); add it and run lake update. COMPARATOR_RECEIPT_NO_MATHLIB=1 declares a project that knowingly has none; the runner then sets VERIFY_COMPARATOR_SKIP_CACHE_GET=1, which the vendored script reads to skip its lake exe cache get (a local change recorded in its header; the slot cache, bound to the script's sha256, is invalidated once). A judge that exits non-zero before judging (no == lake comparator line from verify-comparator.sh, no rejection line from comparator-check.sh) is now reported as the judge tool failed before judging, with its last log line, not as a rejected proof. docs/getting-started.md and docs/comparator.md state the Mathlib requirement. (#62) Changed Documentation gaps from the first stranger test: getting-started step 1 builds a minimal Challenge/Solution project from scratch (module names are file paths; every comparator.json field, definition_names: [] included); README marks the register placeholders and says NAME is the registered name and --path is $HOME-relative; the pre-public install text is gone; the worked example pins Lean v4.35.0-rc2 with toolchain-mechanism output; "about 25 minutes" is the legacy mechanism only; README lists bwrap and explains COMPARATOR_RECEIPT_ALLOWED_HOSTS; commands and expected output are separate blocks. Decision 0006 records the G1 transcript. (#63, #64, #65, #66) public-safety (make public-safety, --strict, history): 0 hit(s) (0 tree, 0 history); 0 blocking, 0 warning(s)

title: Reporting of SMOTE Timing Relative to Data Splitting in Health Prediction Studies: A Systematic Evidence Map, Open Materials
abstract: Open materials for the systematic evidence map ‘Reporting of SMOTE Timing Relative to Data Splitting in Health Prediction Studies’. The study maps how published health prediction studies report the order of SMOTE-family oversampling relative to data splitting, classifying 182 full texts as Pre-splitting, Correct, or Unclear (not recoverable from the text). Candidate records came from the Elicit AI research assistant (search date 8 October 2026) plus citation chasing; this is not a multi-database search. Contents: codebook and decision rules; Elicit query text; coded dataset (FT001–FT182); ID–PDF–DOI map; abstract-stage exclusions (15 records); year-by-timing counts; agreement sensitivity notes; figures; completed PRISMA-ScR checklist. No patient data were used.

title: LASER: Defeasible Certificate Search for Long-Range Protocol Dependencies
abstract: Protocol specifications rarely justify executable behavior in one place: a transition may inherit its source state from a remote control block, name its events only by number, and remain subject to a later correction. Recovering the nearby clause is therefore insufficient; the system must assemble a source-linked certificate and determine whether any stronger rule applies. We introduce LASER, a proof-carrying search method for sparse, defeasible protocol evidence. LASER represents missing support and unresolved corrections as explicit obligations, searches typed evidence routes, and lets an occurrence-aware symbolic checker alone decide whether a certificate warrants, refutes, or leaves a behavior unresolved. On 91 BehaviorCheck families under a matched 2K budget, LASER improves Joint Edge+Proof over the strongest local reader on two model families ($Δ=+.132$, $p=.017$; $Δ=+.198$, $p<.001$) while cutting false discoveries by 2--3$\times$. Controlled replays attribute the gain and its limits: neither reference routing nor deterministic citation expansion alone exceeds the local baseline; whole-document reading (29--65K tokens), two-round iterative retrieval, and even oracle minimal-certificate evidence all fail to reach LASER, localizing the bottleneck in typed obligation closure rather than evidence access. An authority-corruption replay shows source-link errors only cause abstention, while the only unsafe-warrant mechanism is mis-recording a Held erratum as Verified, confined to that erratum's family. LASER thus improves long-range dependency recovery while converting incomplete evidence and uncertain authority into explicit residual obligations rather than unsupported behavior.

title: Control and Value Circulation of Probabilistic AI via Deep-Layer Deterministic Governance AI Connection: Design and Basic Implementation of a Hierarchical Architecture Based on the Casino Protocol (Finalized Edition)
abstract: [Summary of the Paper] Title: Control and Value Circulation of Probabilistic AI via Deep-Layer Deterministic Governance AI Connection: Design and Basic Implementation of a Hierarchical Architecture Based on the Casino Protocol 1. Background and Objective To reconcile the flexibility and expandability of probabilistic AI with definitive resource and governance management that prevents system-wide runaway, this study proposes a hierarchical architecture based on the "Casino Protocol" (Lower Layer: Probabilistic AI / Upper Layer: Deterministic Governance AI). The objective is to define a mathematical model that embeds governance control into the deep foundational layer of AI and to empirically demonstrate its basic operation through algorithms. 2. Clear Categorization of Academic Layers To ensure research validity, the system structure is separated into three distinct layers: Mathematical Layer: Definition of the gateway processing control function G(A) and the 1% value recirculation model (R = rV, V_{\mathrm{net}} = V - R). Implementation Layer (Verification Scope of This Study): Rounding operations maintaining financial precision using Python's standard decimal module (ROUND_HALF_UP) and algorithmic confirmation of conditional branching. System Layer (Future Verification Tasks): Physical power consumption reduction, cryptographic access control, and empirical proof of the economic selection processes of autonomous agents. 3. Key Verification Results Through simulations and implementation tests using a fixed test value (Input value: 572.50), the following results were confirmed: Normal Case (Gateway Passed): Based on the set recirculation rate (r = 0.01), the origin node return amount (5.73) and net value (566.77) were accurately allocated while preserving financial precision (second decimal place). Abnormal Case (Gateway Bypassed): Unpassed processing was structurally rejected as "unproductive energy consumption and exploitation," and the corresponding status was successfully returned via control branching. 4. Conclusion and Outlook This study translates the design philosophy of hierarchical governance based on the Casino Protocol into a reproducible basic implementation (Python code). Future work will focus on system-layer security enhancements (such as preventing flag spoofing) and empirical verification of real-world power and economic impacts.

title: CESNET-TimeSeries26: Multi-year network traffic time series from the CESNET3 ISP network (HDF5 files, part 1 of 4)
abstract: Part 1 of 4 of the HDF5 distribution of CESNET-TimeSeries26 for the CESNET TS-Zoo library. The main record of the dataset is https://zenodo.org/records/21945629 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21945629). Files in this record (48.00 GB, 96 files + SHA256SUMS.txt) CESNET-TimeSeries26-ip_addresses_full-10_minutes.h5.NNN: parts 1–96 of 176 (48.00 GB) SHA256SUMS.txt: SHA-256 of every file above Other parts of this distribution Part 2: https://zenodo.org/records/23280650 Part 3: https://zenodo.org/records/23280754 Part 4: https://zenodo.org/records/23283552 About the dataset CESNET-TimeSeries26 is a multi-year collection of network traffic time series derived from long-term IP-flow monitoring of CESNET3, the Czech national research and education network. It is the successor of CESNET-TimeSeries24 and extends its 40-week collection to 996 days (9 October 2023 – 30 June 2026), which makes annual seasonality, year-over-year drift and model-longevity studies possible on real operational traffic. The dataset has ten source types, each in three aggregations (10 minutes, 1 hour, 1 day), 30 files and 178.7 GB in total: institutions (285 series); institution_subnets (566); ip_addresses_full (278,466, every monitored IP address); ip_addresses_sample (1,000, uniform random sample); five gap-stratified samples ip_addresses_sample_gaps_20_00 … _100_80 (1,000 series each, by the share of missing 10-minute windows); and subnet_longitudinal (135 IP addresses of one institution subnet, 31 December 2021 – 9 July 2026, TCP traffic only, own time grid). Each datapoint is multivariate: numbers of flows, packets and bytes; numbers of unique destination IP addresses, ASNs and transport-layer ports; TCP/UDP and direction ratios of packets and bytes; average flow duration and average TTL. Entity identifiers are pseudonymous integers; no IP addresses, institution names or other identifying information are published. Usage With the library, files and their parts are downloaded from all records, re-assembled and verified automatically: from cesnet_tszoo.datasets import CESNET_TimeSeries26 ds = CESNET_TimeSeries26.get_dataset(data_root="...", source_type="institutions", aggregation="1_hour", dataset_type="time_based") Without the library, download all parts of a split file (they may be spread over several parts of this distribution), concatenate them in numeric order and verify the result: # parts 1–96 in part 1; parts 97–176 in part 2 cat CESNET-TimeSeries26-ip_addresses_full-10_minutes.h5.* > CESNET-TimeSeries26-ip_addresses_full-10_minutes.h5 # expected SHA-256: 042b2fb06fb8fb2c09fa4150d778803ae03ff2ace54f08eb80fead2cda97f987 The downloaded files of this record can be verified with shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS.txt. Citation Please cite the dataset record: CESNET-TimeSeries26. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21945629. The dataset paper is in preparation; until it is published, please also cite: Koumar, J., Hynek, K., Čejka, T., Šiška, P. CESNET-TimeSeries24: Time series dataset for network traffic anomaly detection and forecasting. Scientific Data 12, 338 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-025-04603-x Contact Josef Koumar, Czech Technical University in Prague

The dataset has ten source types, each in three aggregations (10 minutes, 1 hour, 1 day), 30 files and 178.7 GB in total: institutions (285 series); institution_subnets (566); ip_addresses_full (278,466, every monitored IP address); ip_addresses_sample (1,000, uniform random sample); five gap-stratified samples ip_addresses_sample_gaps_20_00 … _100_80 (1,000 series each, by the share of missing 10-minute windows); and subnet_longitudinal (135 IP addresses of one institution subnet, 31 December 2021 – 9 July 2026, TCP traffic only, own time grid). Each datapoint is multivariate: numbers of flows, packets and bytes; numbers of unique destination IP addresses, ASNs and transport-layer ports; TCP/UDP and direction ratios of packets and bytes; average flow duration and average TTL. Entity identifiers are pseudonymous integers; no IP addresses, institution names or other identifying information are published. title: VOICE-AE: automated CTCAE scoring from ambient clinical audio using speech recognition and large language models
abstract: Abstract Treatment-related adverse event documentation is labor-intensive and subject to inter-observer variability. We developed and evaluated VOICE-AE, a multi-stage pipeline integrating automatic speech recognition, speaker diarization and large language models (LLMs) for automated extraction and grading of Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) toxicities from clinician-patient audio recordings. Encounters of prostate cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy were recorded and processed through VOICE-AE. Six blinded human raters independently graded 10 genitourinary/gastrointestinal toxicities from the same transcripts; hierarchical clustering identified an expert-rater subgroup that established the consensus reference standard. A total of 31 patients (39 encounters) were enrolled, yielding 390 encounter–toxicity assessments, of which 300 (76.9%) carried a reference grade of 0. Six-rater Krippendorff alpha was 0.677 for ordinal grading. Against reference standard, VOICE-AE achieved a mean weighted kappa of 0.717 and Krippendorff alpha of 0.669. Exact CTCAE grade match was 82.6% and within-one-grade accuracy 99.2%; because grade 0 predominated, a trivial classifier always predicting grade 0 would achieve 76.9% and 93.6% respectively. Performance was weaker at the grades that drive clinical action (grade 1 F1 0.58; grade 2 F1 0.57), and binary detection sensitivity was 77.8% with specificity 89.0% and precision 68.0%. In a like-for-like comparison restricted to the three expert-cluster raters, mean weighted kappa between VOICE-AE and those experts (0.666) fell just below agreement among the experts themselves (0.681). VOICE-AE performed within the range of inter-expert agreement, supporting the feasibility of automated, post-encounter AE documentation. Accuracy at grade ≥2 and detection of severe toxicity remain unproven.
